overview: La Tène names a widespread Iron Age archaeological culture and artistic tradition, conventionally about 450 to 50 BCE. It included many peoples, not one empire. This record’s 700 to 500 BCE interval is too early, and its small northern French outline cannot represent the wider culture.

periods.title: The imported date mismatch
periods.summary: The displayed interval precedes the conventional La Tène period. The later examples below explain the culture named by this record.

periods.title: Towns and Roman expansion
periods.summary: Fortified towns such as Bibracte developed during the final centuries BCE. Their histories continued through conquest and changes in where people lived.

items.text: At La Salmondière in Brittany, a farming estate developed from around 250 BCE. Curving enclosures surrounded small buildings supported by posts or foundation trenches. This local example puts cultivated land and household work beside the more familiar story of Iron Age warriors.

The same excavation identified a granary carried on four posts from the late Gaulish period. Postholes can reveal the shape of a wooden building long after its walls vanish. A few dark marks in the soil may be what remains of a household’s food store.

At Bibracte, hand mills ground wheat into flour for everyday meals. Producing flour was a task before cooking could even begin. Bread did not start as a tidy bag from a shop; somebody had to work the stone mill first.

sections.title: A busy town with very different homes

items.text: Metalworkers lined the main street near Bibracte’s Rebout gate. One excavated bronze workshop specialised in fibulae, the fasteners used to hold clothing together. A small dress fitting could connect a household’s daily needs with the work of a skilled specialist.

Mount Beuvray has many springs. At the Saint-Pierre spring, excavation revealed a basin dating to the first century BCE, now evoked by a modern reconstruction. Water collection belonged to the town’s practical landscape; the feature should not be confused with a modern tap.

A rich resident’s enormous house at Bibracte, built near the town’s abandonment, had mosaics, wall paintings, baths, wastewater drainage and underfloor heating. These Roman-style comforts belong to a late, wealthy household. They do not prove that every earlier family had its own bathroom.

sections.title: A mirror, a shield and extraordinary craft

items.text: The Desborough mirror from Britain, dated broadly from 50 BCE to 50 CE, used polished bronze for its reflective face. Its back carries intricate engraved curves and textured patterns. This later regional example shows that La Tène art could accompany personal grooming as well as warfare.

The mirror was assembled from a cast handle, a bronze plate and a binding strip around the edge. Its maker may have planned the decoration with compasses. Both faces required skill: one had to reflect an image, while the other was an artwork in its own right.

The Battersea shield facing combines shaped bronze sheets, concealed rivets and 27 red glass studs. Its makers raised the flowing decoration from the metal. Only the decorative metal front survives, not the original wooden shield behind it; the surviving object is beautiful but incomplete.

A gold coin attributed to 52 BCE bears “VERCINGETOR[IX]”, the name Vercingetorix in Latin letters. The brackets mark letters restored by the catalogue editor. This is an actual name on money, not a newly invented Gaulish sentence or a translation of what the pictured person was saying.

Gaulish inscriptions survive from the final years of the third century BCE onward, with later examples continuing under Roman rule. They provide direct evidence of language alongside Greek and Roman accounts. A surviving inscription proves someone wrote it; it does not establish that every child attended a writing school.

At the Swiss site of La Tène, weapons and other remains have inspired different explanations. The Laténium’s recent display presents a reconstructed monument celebrating warrior values in the third century BCE. This is an interpretation of a difficult site, not a surviving eyewitness description of a single ceremony.

Bibracte belonged to a wider growth of fortified towns in the late second century BCE. Workshops, homes and public spaces reveal places where people met and organised work. Within roughly a century of Bibracte’s foundation, Roman expansion had changed the political setting and the town was abandoned.

ending.text: There was no single La Tène kingdom to fall. Conquest and changing settlement patterns reshaped different regions at different times. Bibracte’s abandonment is one local example, while the later British mirror shows that artistic traditions did not stop everywhere at one fixed continental date. The map’s 500 BCE endpoint is much too early.
